title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively You Poured into AI in H1, the Sooner You Get Discounted
dek: A stock market rally needs fresh money to keep buying. Global liquidity is showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
why: This episode ties US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO demand, and household balance sheets into one capital chain, offering a macro framework that doesn't treat AI as a cure-all.
who: For investors tracking both US AI and China/Hong Kong asset allocation, and for primary market practitioners gauging the source and pace of hot money in 2025.
skip: You can skip the case-by-case discussion of Hong Kong IPO pricing; the main thread resumes at 8:11 with the Nvidia liquidity experiment.

points.h: Low IPO break rate is not a good sign
points.body: Don't take the low break rate on Hong Kong IPOs as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year, the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly 50/50 normal level under a market-driven mechanism. That means the participants were mostly short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently, the supply of new listings has shrunk, and some IPO-related funds have run into trouble, but the two newly listed companies still broke issue price, showing that temporary supply-side controls haven't solved the root problem: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

points.h: The more aggressive the AI bet, the sooner the punishment
points.body: Market sentiment reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI capex talk, the higher the valuation. By the end of July, when half-year reports were released, any big internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditures—especially those that burned through free cash flow—got discounted, and even Google wasn't spared. Q2 was the most FOMO quarter across the supply chain; everyone rushed to spend before prices rose, and inventory still supported gross margins. By Q3, inventory is depleted, the price increases hit, and the adverse factors will show up together.

points.h: Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
points.body: Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing shape. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco introduced leasing-to-own to help customers finance purchases, recognizing future revenue as sales upfront. Nvidia is now also pushing leasing-to-own. In its latest report, free cash flow fell by half quarter-over-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels—possibly linked to the credit enhancement and payment structure from leasing-to-own. So Nvidia may have reached a point where it needs more aggressive financial tactics to sustain market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

points.h: Primary market money comes from three-year-old bullets
points.body: The answer lies in fund-raising timing. The money that will be deployed aggressively in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022. From 2023 to 2025, they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets when no one dared and making the most money—the stories of CXMT and YMTC, the two big model companies, and the two big chip companies spurred market-based funds. The mindset is: copy the state's homework. So this is not a rational long-term increment; it's more like a delayed emotional release.

points.h: New property policy unhooks households from the financing chain
points.body: The recent property policy is not about rescuing developers; it's about removing households from the old financing loop. In the past, buying off-plan housing meant households played the role of financing counterparty in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive the home later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers now get completed homes and only act as consumers, resetting risk to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when home prices were near the bottom, to stabilize the asset-side denominator first and avoid panic during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and China's coal and mining consolidation followed similar paths.

points.h: Slow bull is not a slogan; it's about chip structure
points.body: A slow bull isn't achieved by shouting; it's achieved by layering market chips by duration: at the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long-term money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, serving a quasi-stabilization function; China Securities Finance and Central Huijin sit higher, adjusting the index; and at the top are retail investors, private funds, and active management money. New insurance rules require liabilities and assets to match in duration, yield, and liquidity, institutionally ensuring long money invests long, medium money medium, and short money short—not allowing short-term household money to be put into ten-year illiquid assets.

points.h: Crises grow bigger with each bailout; at least one and a half bubbles
points.body: Since the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks have grown accustomed to directly intervening in crises with money printing, acting faster each time. The quantitative easing after 2008 was supposed to clear during the rate-hike cycle, but political intervention interrupted it, and then COVID hit in 2020, so another larger wave of easing was layered on before the previous bubble had dissipated—today we have at least one and a half bubbles accumulated. Central bank governors have learned to print even more money the moment a crisis appears, and the endogenous result is that inflation, financial asset appreciation, and wealth inequality all intensify simultaneously. As long as bubbles aren't allowed to clear, the world may face some form of prolonged stagflation.

quotes.text: The reason I say it's a bit precarious is that today the whole world has a liquidity-peaking problem.
The capital market still thinks whoever spends aggressively is impressive, but when half-year reports come out, it flips to: whoever is aggressive gets punished.
Perhaps Nvidia has also reached a point where, in some sense, it needs to resort to leasing-to-own to drive revenue growth and meet capital market expectations.
Everyone sees that you can pull off that story once, so they think, 'I can definitely pull off that story too'—psychologically, that's about it.
The so-called slow bull we always talk about is not because it is inherently slow and bullish; on the basis of a slow bull, you first need to build a chip structure.
Before the bubble piled up last time had dissipated, an even bigger one was added on top—and it was added without hesitation.
